name: Testosterone pellets (Testopel)

lead: Testosterone pellets are small solid implants placed under the skin that release testosterone gradually. Testopel is the FDA-approved brand; the US approved implantable pellets in 1972 for testosterone deficiency. People choose them to avoid frequent injections or daily gels while keeping the muscle and body-composition benefits of restored testosterone.

The chain: pellets dissolve slowly, steady testosterone enters the bloodstream, and lean mass and fat mass shift in the usual TRT direction. Published work consists mainly of observational serum-level studies, patient-preference surveys and a few small randomised trials in men with diagnosed deficiency. None examine appearance in healthy people.

paras: A clinician inserts the pellets under the skin in a minor office procedure, typically in the hip or buttock area, and they release hormone over several months before the next set is placed. It appeals to people who want infrequent dosing.

The procedure can cause infection or pellet extrusion. As with other testosterone therapy, effects include acne, raised red blood cell counts, sperm suppression and other systemic effects. Compounded pellets are not the same as the branded FDA-approved product.

angle.text: Testosterone pellets are implants under the skin that release hormone for months, used by people on TRT who prefer fewer doses. The looks link is more muscle and less fat from restored testosterone, supported by observational data and small trials in men with deficiency.

lead: Testosterone pellets are small cylindrical implants of crystalline testosterone placed under the skin to provide sustained hormone release. Testopel is the branded product; a 2012 multi-institution study notes that the FDA approved implantable testosterone pellets in 1972 for testosterone deficiency syndrome, and that clinical use was limited until Testopel was reintroduced.[1] A review notes they were not marketed until 2008.[2]

The appearance connection runs through testosterone's effects: restoring levels in men with deficiency is associated with muscle maintenance and growth, and androgenic effects such as body hair, deeper voice and, in some people, acne and scalp hair loss.[3] Pellets appeal to people on testosterone therapy who want steady levels from an implant every 3 to 6 months instead of daily gel or frequent injections.[4][3]

Medication references list pellet doses of 150 to 1,200 mg every 3 to 6 months for men, in strengths of 50 to 200 mg per pellet.[3] Evidence consists of observational serum-level studies, patient-preference surveys and small randomised trials, mostly in men with diagnosed hypogonadism.[1][4][5] No published trials have examined pellets for appearance outcomes in healthy people.

paras: Pellets are used for testosterone replacement in men with deficiency [1]. A single-centre trial also compared compounded and branded pellets in men with testosterone deficiency [5]. A registered phase 1 trial tested pellets together with vitamins D and E in Peyronie's disease [6].

A multi-institution observational study combined databases from six academic centres to characterise serum testosterone levels after Testopel insertion [1]. A randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial compared a compounded pellet (E100) with Testopel in men with testosterone deficiency to assess both safety and efficacy [5]. A further phase 3 registration compares Testopel with generic pellets in 75 men [7].

A review of pellet therapy describes decay kinetics, pituitary suppression and effects on other sex steroids following insertion, noting that older pharmacokinetic work was on a different formulation (Organon pellets) but informs Testopel.[2] A 1990 randomised study characterised pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of pellets in men.[8]

Older reports noted relatively high rates of pellet extrusion and infection with Organon pellets; a randomised trial in 1999 tested whether washing pellets to remove surface particles reduced extrusion.[9][10] A 2009 single-site retrospective analysis reported safety and limited efficacy data from patients treated with Testopel.[10]
A survey-based study of 175 men at an academic urology practice examined what led patients to start or stop pellets compared with gels and injections [4].

On T Nation, a 2010 thread asks for Testopel experiences and includes a user saying the quarterly implant was the least laborious method compared with gel, and another posting that he had used it for three years.[11] Another poster says insurance began accepting Testopel and compares costs of pellets from a compounding pharmacy.[12] Other users in the same communities favour injections or note high measured levels on pellets and discuss individual lab results.[13]

General testosterone therapy effects include acne, oily skin and hair loss, sperm suppression, and warnings related to cardiovascular events, prostate conditions and blood pressure; testosterone is contraindicated in pregnancy [3]. Implantation is a minor surgical procedure, which makes procedure-related events such as infection a topic in the pellet literature.

Wikipedia lists common testosterone effects as acne, swelling and breast enlargement in men, with serious risks including liver toxicity and heart disease, and notes a February 2025 FDA label change that removed cardiovascular language from the boxed warning and added a blood pressure warning.[3] A 2021 case report examined Testopel therapy and laboratory assay interpretation.[14]

Pellets are offered through urology and hormone clinics and are also prepared by compounding pharmacies, which the 2023 trial compared against the branded product [5]. Testosterone is a controlled substance in the US [3].

Brand lists for testosterone products include Testopel among injections, gels and patches.[3] In the US it is Schedule III, in the UK Class C, and prescription-only in the EU.[3] Pellets are also used in transmasculine hormone therapy and are approved in the UK for postmenopausal women, according to Wikipedia.[3]

Observational data show serum testosterone levels after Testopel insertion across six academic centres [1]. A 2023 randomised trial compared compounded and branded pellets [5], and a phase 3 trial (NCT04523480, 75 men, completed) compared Testopel with generic pellets [7]. A phase 1 trial (NCT01578473, 75 participants) tested pellets for Peyronie's disease [6]. No studies found for appearance or physique outcomes in healthy people.
Earlier trials include the 1999 randomised extrusion study and the 1990 pharmacokinetic randomised trial; men's contraception trials have also used testosterone pellets with progestins.[8][9][15]
